Yes. The story builds its insight on the surveying benchmark: a brass disk set in bedrock that still reports the same coordinates while the continent carries it away. It turns this into a fresh metaphor for human drift. His daughter, his ex-wife and his younger self have all moved while the old "numbers" stay stamped as if nothing changed.

It pairs this with a second striking idea: the strange solitude of being the only person who has "crossed over" into the world where the woman is dead, while everyone else, including whoever keeps calling her phone, still lives in the world where she is alive. These ideas come through concrete, unfamiliar details such as continental drift, lichens and library due dates, rather than familiar platitudes about grief. As a result, an average reader is likely to come away with a new way of thinking about loss, connection and unnoticed change.
